description: Perennial much branched shrubs up to 1.3 m tall; stems glabrous or pilose at least when young; leaves trullate to ovate, glabrous to pubescent, dentate, petiolate; peduncles sometimes striate, slightly enlarged at the apex, often hollow; heads slightly concave at the juncture with the peduncle, otherwise hemispherical; phyllaries nu- merous, indurate upon maturity, 2-3 seriate, sometimes foliar, subulate, convex, spreading at maturity; ray flowers female and fertile, yellow, turning reddish to maroon upon aging, 2-3-lobed at apex, fully and firmly fused to the achene, style bifid, reddish branches recurved; ray achenes 3-angled, obpyramidal, with a long, stout, free awn on the inner angle; disk flowers numerous, of nearly uniform width, glabrous, yellow, 5-lobed, lobes vein-thickened at the periphery, anthers free sagittate at the bases, with sterile appendages at the apices, branches of the bifid styles with trullate, inconspicuously velutinous appendages; disk achenes 2-4-angled, flattened to obpyramidal with 1-4 unequal stout awns; palea uncinate or simply acuminate at apex, keeled dorsally, concave and conduplicate, about equalling or exceeding the disk flowers; receptacle conical; x = 28.
bibliographicCitation: Torres, Andrew M. 1970. Revision of the genus Philactis (Compositae). Brittonia. 21: 322-331.

description: Aerial hemiparasites on trees and shrubs; plants evergreen, much-branched, shrublike. Stems usually swollen at the nodes. Leaves opposite, foliaceous or in a few species reduced to connate, deltoid scales. Plants glabrous or pubescent. Infloreseence a jointed axillary or terminal ( ?) spike. Plants dioecious or monoecious, the flowers unisexual and sunken along the rachis. Calyx 3- (or rarely 2-4) lobed, the sepals distinct, deltoid. Staminiate flower with a sessile 2-chambered anther opposite the base of each sepal. Pistillate flower epigynous, with 1 style; stigma eapitate; ovary 1-chambered, the calyx adnate to the ovary, persistent in fruit. Fruit a drupe (but without an obviously hardened endocarp), 1-seeded with a glutinous, mucilaginous mesocarp, usually white, rarely red.
bibliographicCitation: Wiena, Delbert. 1964. Revision of the acatophyllous species of Phoradendron. Brittonia. 16: 11-54.

description: Monotypic. Shrubs ca. 1 m tall, with scattered coarse stellate pubescence. Leaves petiolate (the petioles progressively shorter upward), the blades ovate to suborbicular, deeply cordate, crenate, obtuse or subacute, with scattered stellate-pubescence, the hairs smaller on the upper than on the lower surface; stipules filiform, inconspicuous. Flowers solitary in the axils of reduced leaves (floral bracts) on long lateral flowering branches; pedicels 1 cm long or less; involucel of 8 filiform bracts, ca. half the length of the calyx; calyx 1.5 cm long, ca. half-divided, coarsely pubescent; petals 2- 3 times the length of calyx, rose (or whitish) with dark red center and venation, glabrous; androecium included, the column glabrous, apically 5-dentate, the filaments arising at 3 distinct levels on column; styles 10, the stigmas capitate. Fruits schizocarpic; mericarps 5, carinate and reticulately rugose, divided into two cells, the solitary seed in the upper cell, the lower cell empty, with irregular partitions; seeds 3.5 mm long, with tufts of hairs at either end of hilum. Chromosome number unknown.
bibliographicCitation: Fryxell, Paul A. 1997. The American genera of Malvaceae --- II. Brittonia. 49: 204-269.

description: Trees, reproductive height 5-40 m; wood described in Miller (1991). Stipules deciduous; leaves petiolate, simple (perhaps unifoliolate); petioles terete, bearing proximal and distal pulvini that are nearly equal in length; leaf blades entire, ovate, elliptic or obovate, to broadly elliptic or broadly obovate, 3- to 1 1-pal- minerved at base, penninerved distally, membranous or coriaceous, sparsely to densely stellate- or peltate-tomentose abaxially (Fig. 2). Flowers solitary, acti- nomorphic to slightly zygomorphic, produced opposite the leaves (perhaps terminal on each sympodial branch segment); pedicels initially 2- or 3-bracteolate, the bracteoles often deciduous before flowering; calyx tubular, conical or narrowly campanulate, sometimes zygomorphic, broadly 3-5-lobed at summit, densely tomentulose without, densely velutinous with pale, ascending trichomes within, persistent and often accrescent in fruit; petals 5, spathulate or linear-spathulate, yellow to ochraceous or ferrugineous-yellow (reportedly also white), usually pilose or tomentose; staminal tube long-exsert from the corolla, bearing 5 linear lobes at summit (Fig. 1), antheriferous at apex of tube and on abaxial surface of the recurved or spreading, actinomorphic (sometimes zygomorphic?) lobes, glabrous or tomentose, often bearing vermiform, uniseriate, multicellular trichomes (Fig. 1B; cf. Fig. 1 in Cuatrecasas, 1971); thecae 15-30, straight or vermiform, longitudinally bilocular, the uppermost often paired and parallel; locules of anthers trans versely septate to form 3 to many angular or rounded foveae, the foveae of the two adjacent locules often alternating and overlapping (Figs. 1, 5C); pollen de- scribed by Nilsson and Robyns (1986); ovary superior, 5-locular, each locule biovulate; style filiform, often equalling or exceeding the staminal lobes, mildly to strongly zygomorphic, longitudinally 5-sulcate, the exsert portion densely to- mentose; stigma actinomorphic or zygomorphic, capitate to shallowly 5-lobed. Fruits drupaceous, ovoid, ellipsoid or depressed-globose; exocarp coriaceous, densely tomentulose; mesocarp moist, densely fibrous; endocarp bony-fibrous, persistent along with the innermost fibers of the mesocarp to form a protective cover around the seeds (the "nucula" of Simpson, 1982); pedicel of fruit usually stout, sometimes slender, ebracteolate, ligneous; calyx of fruit patelliform to shal- lowly or deeply cupulate, ligneous, the margin entire to erose, irregularly toothed or broadly lobed. Seeds 5 per fruit, or fewer by abortion, elongate, bluntly angular to nearly terete in cross section; testa membranous, brown; seedlings known from a single species (P. mammosa) of"durian morphology" sensu Ng (1978), a seedling type previously unknown in neotropical Bombacaceae.
bibliographicCitation: Alverson, William S. 1991. A synopsis of Phragmotheca (Bombacaceae), with two new species and a new sub-species. Brittonia. 43: 73-87.

description: Vascularization (Fig. 7, A-P). -The following differences can be drawn from the Lycium pattern: 1) lateral sepal branches are not accompanied by very small gaps (Fig. 7E); 2) all sepal supplies have a quite horizontal pattern immediately after diverging because the calyx is broadly campanulate (Fig. 7A, E); 3) just after the staminal bundles differentiate, the vascular tissue, instead of forming a con- tinuous ring, divides into 10 or 1 1 separate strands (Fig. 71, J), from which four ventral, two dorsal and a number of lateral ovarian traces arise. Calyx. -Broadly campanulate and pubescent with uniseriate, glandular trichomes, the heads and stalks of which are many-celled and variable in length. The calyx envelops the berry. The inner epidermis from the basal plane zone is secretory, with one- or many-layered sessile glands, and occasionally glandular trichomes (Figs. 6F, G; 7A, F, G, H). Secretory cells have thick walls and are elongated, quite isodiametric, and have plenty of small vacuoles. In the basal zone, the regions corresponding to median sepal bundles are higher than internervate ones, which are somewhat hollow (Fig. 7F, G). Corolla. -Largely infundibuliform, yellowish or yellowish-white. The corolla-tube is pubescent without and within, mainly in the region of stamen adnation. The corolla lobes are short, ciliate, and two to three times broader than long. As in Grabowskia, the corolla is entirely caducous and does not leave a ring of tissue as in Lycium. An exclusive feature is the plicate corolla aestivation. Androecium. -Filaments are subequal and densely hairy at the base. They are cylindrical but somewhat enlarged at the base with thin appendages that can only be seen in thin sections (Fig. 7M). Filaments are adnate to the corolla-tube in their lower third. Anther dehiscence belongs to "type 1" (Bernardello, 1983b) but I could not observe the number of layers of the sutural zone. Morphologicalflower type. -There is little variation in flowers of Phrodus species, all of them with the same morphological type. The gynoecium shows the typical structure of the family and possesses, in the ovary base, a manifest red nectary with two extensions at the top (Bernardello, 1986).

description: Phyllocarpus Riedel ex Endlicher is the only American caesalpinioid legume with distichous, once paripinnate leaves, brilliant red, glabrous flowers borne on defoliate branches, diadelphous stamens, and flat samaroid pods winged along the seminiferous suture. The fruit has been compared with that of papilionoid Lonchocarpus or Derris. Cowan and Polhill (1981: 133) admitted two species and referred the genus to the informally defined Brownea group, but it is morphologically isolated there and its true affinities are not apparent, though it bears some similarity (Gunn, 1991: 95, 166, 1540) to the Caesalpinieae and Cassiinae. Britton and Rose (1930: 219) proposed a group, Phyllocarpeae (without stated rank), to accommodate it. The dispersal of Phyllocarpus is singular: seasonally dry woodland in Central America; the Puru's basin in southern Amazonian Brazil; and vicinity of Rio de Janeiro, the type locality. At the time (1912) that Phyllocarpus was discovered in Guatemala, about 6000 km distant from Rio de Janeiro, it was very naturally interpreted as a second species, Ph. septentrionalis. However, the differential characters listed by J. Donnell Smith, supposedly less numerous and larger leaflets coinciding with larger flowers, are not confirmed in subsequently collected material. In Central  America the leaflets are generally 3-5, rarely 6 pairs, and the largest are 4-8 X 2.5- 3.5 cm, whereas at Rio the leaflets are mostly 5-7 pairs and the larger ones ca. 3-5 X 1.5-1.9 cm. Individual leaves from these remotely distant regions are essentially identical (compare Campos Porto in RJ 23653 with Hughes 1224, both NY), whereas the material from Rio Puru's is absolutely indistinguishable from some Guatemalan specimens. The fruits are essentially uniform in all particulars. Nothing justifies retention of P. septentrionalis, even at infraspecific rank.

description: Shrubs; bark smooth, light grayish brown; wood cream-white. Stipules interpetiolar, sheathing and connected to the petioles, persistent. Leaves short-petiolate, blades obovate to oblanceolate, decurrent at base, acute to rounded at apex; domatia absent. Inflorescences axillary, 1-2 per node, cymose, pauciflorous. Flowers protandrous, long pedicellate; hypanthium obconical. Calyx papery, entire or lobed, with a ring of white pilose hairs at base inside, expanding into a rotate pterophyll after anthesis. Corolla funnelform, white; tube funnelform, glabrous throughout; lobes 4-5(-6), oblong, rounded at apex; aestivation imbricate. Stamens alternate to the petals, half-exserted among the petals; anthers narrowly oblong-elliptic, dorsifixed near the base, dehiscing by longitudinal slits; filaments attached near the mouth, extremely short, glabrous throughout. Style exserted; style branches opening after complete maturity of the anthers, ovate, reflexed at maturity. Ovary 2-celled, with one seed per locule basally inserted. Fruits pseudosamaras, narrowly cylindrical, multicostate, indehiscent, with a rotate entire or lobed pterophyll developed from the whole calyx. Seeds with basal hilum, clavate, fleshy, smooth.

description: Shrubs or small trees, infrequently epiphytic, glabrous throughout, the young twigs variously grooved. Leaves alternate, petiolate, elliptic to narrowly ovate, or infre- quently narrowly obovate; apex acuminate to long acuminate, the acumen sometimes very narrow at its junction with the blade; base acute, cuneate, or obtuse, narrowly decurrent onto the petiole; margins entire to distinctly serrate. Stipules small, with glandular hairs on the inner surface. Inflorescences cymose and branched or racemose and essentially unbranched above the point of insertion, arising on the midvein on the adaxial leaf surface anywhere near the middle of the blade to the base of the acumen or, less frequently, on the acumen. Flowers 2-4 mm in diameter; sepals 5, usually with minute teeth or fimbriae on the margins; petals 5, valvate in bud, spreading or reflexed at anthesis, with an inconspicuous midvein; stamens 5, alterni- petalous, first erect then reflexed, alwvays shorter than the petals, the anthers 2-celled dehiscing by lateral slits; ovary unilocular, with 2 intruding parietal placentae, the ovules campylotropous, horizontally oriented, the style usually bifid, 0.2-0.6 mm long. Fruit a globose or subglobose berry, white at maturity. Seeds oblong, the seed coat tuberculate, the hilum centric to acentric but never terminal, the embryo straight, with 2 cotyledons, albuminous.

description: Eight species. Shrubs or small trees, densely tomentose, the stellate hairs often stipitate. Leaves petiolate, the blades 3-7 lobed (or merely 3-7-angular), the central lobe the largest, cordate, crenate to subentire, obtuse, acute, or acuminate; stipules subulate. Peduncles solitary in the leaf axils, usually exceeding the subtending leaves, 1- to many-flowered, often umbellate, the branch sometimes forming a terminal panicle; involucel trimerous, the bracts distinct and lanceolate to ovate or forming a gamophyllous tube, sometimes caducous; calyx plicate in bud, 5-lobed, to- mentose; petals showy, lavender or red, sometimes white; androecium included, filamentiferous at apex, glabrous, pallid, the pollen yellow or orange; styles 10-40, sometimes strigose; stigmas obliquely cap- itate or introrsely decurrent. Fruits schizocarpic, globose to oblate, tomentose; mericarps 10-40, reniform, thin, dehiscent, 2-3-seeded; seeds reniform, glabrous. 2n = 34 (3 species).

description: Shrubs or small trees 0.5-4.0 m tall. Leaves palmately trifoliolate, petiolate; stipels absent; stipules opposite the petiole, fused for 2/3 their length or more, the bifid apices acute. Inflorescence a loose or congested axillary or terminal raceme. Flowers pedicellate, yellow, arising 3 at a node, each from the base of a con- spicuous bract. Calyx 5-lobed, the 2 uppermost lobes fused for most of their length; with age most of the calyx disarticulating (along with the petals and sta- mens) at the perigyneal line of the flower. Corolla papilionate; banner slightly longer than wide, notched at the apex, the claw prominent. Stamens 10, separate. Ovary linear, glabrous to pubescent, 3-10-ovulate. Fruit a linear, flattened, 2-10-seeded, thin to somewhat leathery pod; seeds flattened, obliquely elliptical, the radicle incurved. Base chromosome number, x = 9.

description: Bulbous perennial herb of primary, midelevation rain forest. Bulb subglobose, 5-6 cm long, 5-5.5 cm diam. with light brown tunics, apically articulated into a short neck, producing offsets at the base. Leaves 1-5, persistent, petiolate; petiole 7-22.5 cm long; lamina elliptic, 26.5-45.5 cm long, 11.5- 16.5 cm wide, attenuate at the base, shortly acuminate at the apex, fairly thin-textured, slightly plicate, with 10-12 veins on either side of the midrib. Inflorescence (Figs. 1B, 3A, B) scapose and umbellate (reduced hel- icoid cymes); scape 49-66 cm tall, ca. 0.5 cm diam. at base, terete, solid, slightly glau- cous, bearing 10-41 flowers subtended and enclosed before anthesis by two lanceolate, greenish white and quickly marcescent bracts ca. 4 cm long and 0.5 cm wide at base; inner bracteoles successively smaller and narrower. Flowers (Figs. C, 3C, D) 2.5- 3 cm long, protandrous, pedicellate, without noticeable fragrance; pedicels 1.5-2 cm long, thin; perianth zygomorphic, white, consist- ing of 6 tepals in two whorls of 3, basally connate into a short, funnelform green tube 0.5-0.7 cm long, ca. 2 mm wide at the base dilating to ca. 4 mm at the throat; all tepals ascendant or 4-5 abruptly ascendant and 1- 2 declinate or spreading horizontally; outer tepals 20-25 mm long, 2.5-3.5 mm wide, obliquely lanceolate, apiculate; inner tepals 15-20 mm long, 3.5-5 mm wide, obliquely elliptic-lanceolate, obtuse at apex. Stamens 6, connate at the base into a short, cylindrical staminal cup; cup 3-4 mm long, 2- 2.5 mm wide, slightly declinate, white, with 1 bifid or 2 entire teeth between each free filament (Fig. 3E); teeth 1.5-2 mm long; free filaments slightly 3-seriate in length, 6-10 mm long, ca. 1 mm wide at base, filiform, white, slightly ascendant at first then strongly declinate; anthers 2.8-3.2 mm long, versatile, introrse; pollen white, grain boat- shaped elliptic, monosulcate, exine finely reticulate. Style 1.4-1.6 mm long, white, declinate then ascendant distally as stigma becomes receptive; stigma 0.5 mm wide, capitate, papillose. Ovary ellipsoidal, ca. 5 mm long, ca. 3 mm wide, green, slightly trigonous, trilocular, with (1)2(3) basal, anatropous ovules in each locule. Fruit a loculi- cidal capsule, green, turning dull light yel- low to pale orange-green at dehiscence; pedicel in fruit 2-3 cm long; capsule ca. 1.1 cm diam.; seeds 1 per locule, ellipsoidal, turgid, ca. 1.1 cm long, 0.8 cm wide, with a lustrous, black, smooth, phytomelanous testa. Monotypic.

description: Perennial, erect scapose to leafy-stemmed herb 12-57 cm high from lignescent branching caudex ordinarily covered with old leaf petioles; adventitious shoots from ramifying root system. Roots 2-10 mm in diameter. Stems single or branching above and glabrous to puberulent with no to numerous short- to long-stipitate glands. Lower leaves alternate and frequently basal with blades inconspicuously 3-5-nerved, glabrous to densely pubescent, coriaceous, narrowly to broadly lanceolate, ovate, elliptic, obovate or occasionally almost round, entire or very rarely trifid with con- tracted bases which are decurrent into the margined petiole, blade 18-100 mm long and 4.5-38 mm wide with petiole 3-60 mm long, more or less pubescent, often im- pressed-punctate with exudate in the depressions, blade tips acute, acuminate or obtuse; upper leaves somewhat reduced in size and then lanceolate, ovate, elliptic or strongly reduced to narrowly acute; bracts lanceolate or oval. Inflorescence a few- to several-headed cymose panicle, each stem bearing 1-11 heads; peduncles 2.5-140 mm long. Heads radiate, hemispheric to campanulate; involucre of 9-21 equal or subequal bracts in two series, bracts lanceolate, oblong, elliptic, ovate, obovate, or spatulate and flat or slightly cupped, tips acute, acuminate, obtuse or caudate- attenuate; receptacle naked, flat to slightly convex. Ray florets 6-12, pistillate and fertile with yellow oblong, obovate, elliptic or strap-shaped ligules 3-11 mm wide and 6-16 mm long; ligule tip tridentate or rarely obtuse; tube glandular. Disc florets 25-83 with regular corollas, yellow, few to numerous sessile or short- to long- stipitate glands especially on tube and throat; corolla 3-6.5(7.5) mm long; tube 1-2.7 mm long; throat 1.5-3.8 mm long, cylindric, cylindro-campanulate, occasionally funnel-form, or rarely campanulate; lobes 5, equal, 0.5-1.4 mm long, usually reflexed after anthesis; anthers partially exserted in mature florets, more or less sagittate at the base with an ovate terminal appendage; style branches recurved, subterete with somewhat enlarged papillose apices, stigmatic lines marginal on inner surface; achenes 1-8 mm long, black to tan, narrowly obpyramidal and 4-sided, both angles and faces with few to numerous hairs (faces occasionally glabrous), pappus of 8-16 linear lanceolate, lanceolate, oblanceolate, oval or elliptic scales with tips acute, obtuse or truncate, 0.2-0.7 mm wide and 0.6-3.7 mm long, margins lacerate and midribs stopping well below apex or becoming excurrent as a short scabrous awn. 2n = 24.

description: Erect, unarmed, slender to robust annuals or rarely perennials, to 6 (-10) dm tall, viscid-pubescent with rank odor, simple or branched. Leaves 3-foliolate, petiolate; leaflets entire, to 6 cm long; stipules linear and gland-like, minute, present and visible in all species in the apical meristematic region, in older portions becoming obsolete. Racemes terminal, strongly elongating in fruit, the bracts 1- to 3-foliolate, smaller than the leaves. Corolla open in the bud; sepals free to the base, deciduous; petals spatulate to obcordate or obvate, clawed to almost sessile, truncate or emarginate to erose or laciniate, white, cream, or pink to magenta (or yellow ?), dimorphic, the adaxial pair longer; gland between corolla and androecium prominent, strictly adaxial, either solid and with obliquely truncate to concave apex, or tubular, orange or red; stamens (6-) 8-27, of unequal length largely because of staggered maturation, the abaxial shorter and maturing last; style slender; stigma minute or very slightly capitate; fruit a many-seeded, elongate, erect, sessile or subsessile silique; valves dehiscing apically and incompletely, persistent in fruit. Seeds subspherical, the cleft formed by the invagination of the testa narrow but part-way open.

description: Mostly erect perennial herbs or trees to more than 12 m tall; stems terete, angular or canaliculate, to 20 cm thick; bark of large species becoming rough on older stems; at least the lower leaves opposite, entire to deeply lobed, pinnately or palmately veined, sessile or petiolate, the petiole sometimes winged; heads solitary to many; phyllaries usually 4-6 in 1-2 series; ray flowers in 1 or rarely 2 series, carpellate, the corollas 2-3-lobed or entire, yellow, white, or orange-red; ray paleae usually concave, the tip sometimes acuminate; disc flowers staminate, of about the same number as or many more than the ray flowers; corollas tubular, usually or sometimes purplish at least when dried; pappus wanting; disc paleae usually chartaceous or infrequently of firmer texture and subulate, with or without prom- inent veins; receptacle flattened, somewhat to decidedly convex; achenes brown, purplish black, or black, obovoid or spherical and slightly flattened laterally, or 3-5-angled, the angles infrequently winged, to 7 mm long; receptacle flat or convex.

description: Lianas (or slender trees or shrubs with scandent branehes), glabrous throughout, the branches and branehlets usually opposite, sometimes alternate, slender, subterete, slightly swollen at nodes, lenticellate; leaves opposite, petiolate, the petioles slender, shallowly canaliculate, the leaf-blades usually greenish when dried, decurrent on the petiole, the veinlets copiously reticulate and prominulous on both surfaces; flowers small, in distal dichotomies or congested in groups of 2-5 at apices of ultimate branchlets, subtended by ininute bracteoles similar to bracts, pedicellate; sepals 5, imbricate, rounded or obtuse at apex; petals 5, spreading or erecto-pateilt, thin- carnose to submembranous, yellowish, rounded at apex; disk carnose, inconspicuous, forming an annular-pulvinate cushion below stamens, slightly projecting, often hardly distinguishable from ovary, rarely elevated on upper margin and free from ovary at apical margin; stamens 3, suberect to spreading, the filaments membranous, the anthers basifixed, extrorsely nutant, transversely ellipsoid, dehiscing by extrorse-apical horizontal confluent clefts; ovary depressed-trigonous, soon conspicuously 3-lobed, the style short, obtuse or minutely capitate, the stigmiias obscure or mainute and alternate with staimens, the locules 3, the ovules 2-8 per locule, collateral or in superposed pairs, aseendinlg from the inner basal angle; fruiting infloreseence swollen, the fruits usually several per infloreseenee, capsular, the capsules 3, divergent, erecto-patent, separately attached to a swollen receptacle, flattened on both surfaces, obtuse or subacute and slightly swollen at base, sharp and entire at margins and often appearing distally winged, dehiscing along an inconspicuous median suture, the pericarp thin-coriaceous or papyraceous; seeds 2-8, probably completely occupying the capsule- cavity at maturity, erect from base, affixed by a conspicuous basal wing, the enibryoniferous portion apical, coriaceous, somewhat flat- tened, the wing membranous, obtuse at base and affixed by a small obdeltoid funicle, traversed by a conspicuous longitudinal nerve near center, often conspicuously thickened distally on inner margin, the raphe ascending along the outer margin of wing, distally conspicuous.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, A. C. 1940. Hippocrateaceae. Brittonia. 3 (3): 356-367.

description: Nineteen species. Shrubs or subshrubs, the stems usually densely stellate-pubescent (glabrescent in P. thurberi), sometimes also with long simple hairs. Leaf blades ovate to elliptic, basally cordate to truncate, crenate- serrate (rarely subentire), acute or acuminate, minutely pubescent (glabrescent in P. thurberi), sometimes with long appressed simple hairs, at least on upper surface; petioles much shorter than the blades to sub- equal to the blades; stipules subulate or linear, 1-11 mm long. Flowers solitary or glomerate in the axils, or borne in small axillary umbels, sometimes aggregated into terminal inflorescences, the pedicels short or long and slender; calyx basally rounded, small, ecostate, about half-divided, stellate pubescent and sometimes also with long simple hairs, sometimes with glandular hairs; petals yellow (rarely white), 4-15 mm long; staminal column shorter than corolla, pallid, usually more or less stellate pubescent, sometimes glabrous, the filaments short; styles 5-10, with capitellate stigmas. Fruits 5-10 mm diam., stellate-pubescent or hirsute; mericarps 5-10, apically acute to spinescent, with or without an endoglossum, the lateral walls sometimes striate-reticulate basally, 3-seeded. 2n = 16, 32
bibliographicCitation: Fryxell, Paul A. 1997. The American genera of Malvaceae --- II. Brittonia. 49: 204-269.

description: Semishrub with ovate serrulate petioled leaves and subulate stipules. Inflorescence racemose-paniculate, with spreading-ascending pedicels anid leafy spreadinlg lanceolate bracts. Sepals 4, nearly or quite distinct, subequal, nlarrow. Petals 4, sessile, narrow, the upper 2 ascending-erect, the lower 2 lateral and inrolled abont 1/3 their length. Stamens and style free, long-exserted, the sterile stamen somewhat petaloid, the fertile one fleshy. Stigma subeapitate. Capsule subglobose, 4-loculed.
bibliographicCitation: Munz, Philip A. 1961. The Lopezieae (Onagraceae). Brittonia. 13 (1): 73-90.

description: Unarmed, deciduous, polygamo-dioecious erect or spreading shrubs or small trees; foliage usually strongly aromatic, glandular-punctate with pellucid dots; leaves alternate, without stipules, digitate, trifoliate (rarely 5-foliate), the leaflets jointed to the petiole; winter buds pubescent, more or less covered by the base of the petiole. Infloreseences terminal, on short leafy branchlets which may be borne laterally or at the ends of branches of the past season; branchlets with usually 3-5 leaves; flowers greenish white, appearing with the leaves, several to many in usually compound clusters, mostly unisexual by abortion, with vestigial parts of the opposite sex usually present. Sepals 4 or 5 (-6), 1-2 mm long, pubescent to glabrous on the outside, glabrous on the inside, soon deciduous; petals distinct, imbricated in the bud, of the same number as the sepals and alternate with them, usually more than twice  as long, commonly 4-5 (-6) mm long, oval or ovate to elliptic or linear-oblong, always hirsute on the inside, especially about the middle above the base, usually with at least a marginal band of fine pubescence outside. Stamens as many as the petals and alternate with them, in mature staminate flowers generally as long as the petals, in pistillate flowers generally reduced to vestiges of filaments and small imperfect anthers; filaments commonly flattened about the middle and expanded laterally, more or less hirsute with long white hairs (glabrous in one species) ; anthers oblong-ovate to elliptic, cordate at base, 2-celled, introrse, the cells splitting longitudinally. Pistils, in both pistillate and staminate flowers, raised on short disc-like gynophores situated between the stamens and ovary as though replacing an inner whorl of stamens (Moore, J. A., New Phyt. 35: 320. 1936), often lobed in the staminate flowers; ovaries compressed, 2 (-3)-locular; styles terminal, 1 mm long or less, jointed to the tops of the ovaries; stigmas more or less 2 (-3)-lobed; ovules 2 in each locule, inserted one above the other, the upper one only develop- ing into a seed; pistils abortive in staminate flowers, the style usually obsolete, a stigma sometimes present. Fruit a 2 (-3)-carpellate indehiseent samara surrounded more or less completely by a reticulated wing (teratological modifications are often found; cf. Harris, J. A., Bull. Torrey Club 38: 385-387. 1911); pericarp very tough and coriaceous at maturity, partly continuous into the wings; endocarp hard, thin, very tenacious about the seed in mature fruit; seed oblong, covered by a smooth, dark-colored, thin and rather brittle testa, generally one in each locule, attached basally by a short raphe; embryo straight, the cotyledons oblong-oval, plane, the radiele superior; endosperm fleshy, white. Indications of nucellar embryo development and a nuclear endosperm have been found by Mauritzon (Svensk Bot. Tidskr. 29: 319-347. 1935).
bibliographicCitation: Bailey, Virginia L. 1962. Revision of the genus Ptelea (Rutaceae). Brittonia. 14: 1-45.

description: Hypanthium tubular, conspicuously winged, the wings spinoseciliate, sepals erect, ovate-lanceolate, becoming subcoriaceous in fruit; anthers isomorphic, the prolonged connective 2-tuberculate at base. Erect, branching, annual herbs, with angled stems, oblong to laneolate leaves, and flowers of moderate size in terminal trichotomous eymes. Three or four species of northern South America, of which only the following is known to occur within our limits.

description: Much resembling Tibouchina and distinguished from it chiefly by habit and the presence of large branched hairs on the hypanthium. Herbaceous or partly woody plants, often of weedy aspect and habits, with hispid or strigose stems, lanceolate to ovate-oblong leaves, and medium-sized flowers in terminal clusters, panicles, or nearly solitary in the upper axils. The hairs on the stem in the first two are distinctly geniculate or prolonged backward at base into a short spur. About 30 species ranging throughout tropical America, but nost numerous in Brazil.

description: Herbaceous, glabrous annuals with fibrous roots. Stems erect and branching. Leaves petiolate with filiform, decompound divisions or reduced to terete, hollow, septate phyllodia. Petioles sheathing the stem; border narrow, hyaline. Inflorescence compound. Peduncles terminal or axillary. Involucre of enitire or pinnatifid bracts, conspicuous or inconspicuous. Rays few to numerous. Flowers white, rarely pink. Calyx-teeth small, lanceolate or deltoid. Styles the same length as to very much longer than the conie stylopodium. Carpophore 2-cleft about one-half of its lenlgth. Schizoearp orbicular or suborbicular. Dorsal ribs of the carpel conspicuous, rounded or acute; secondary ribs none; lateral ribs inconspicuous, separate from the corky tissue on the coinmissural side of the rib. Corky tissue forming a conspicuous or inconspicuous longitudinal band around the fruit. Oil tube solitary between the ribs, 2 on the commissural side.
bibliographicCitation: Easterly, Nathan W. 1957. A morphological study of Ptilimnium. Brittonia. 9: 136-145.

description: Shrubs or small trees 1-8 m. high, or sometimes reputedly vines; leaves alternate, pinnately compound; leaflets 3-7, commonly 5, opposite; rachis conspicuously winged; infloreseence a long raceme, rarely paniculate at the base; pedicels strongly jointed a little below the flower; flowers perfect; sepals 5, joined at the very base or apparently distinct; petals 5, distinct, glabrous on the outside, sparsely short-hairy near the base witlhin, not spreading at anthesis; stamens 10, with long slender-filaments each bearing a very short hairy appendage at the base; carpels 5, weakly united, born on an evident short gynophore; style 1, long and slender, the part from each carpel discernible; stigma essentially capitate; fruit of several distinct drupes.
bibliographicCitation: Cronquist, Arthur J. 1944. Studies in the Simaroubaceae--IV. Resumé of the American genera. Brittonia. 5: 128-147.

description: Shrubs or small trees to 13 m tall. Leaves opposite, 1- or 3-foliolate, petiolate; blade entire, chartaceous to coriaceous. Inflores- cence a cauline (rarely in axils of extant leaves), pedunculate, circinate raceme, 1-4 at a node, often elongating considerably as successive flowers develop. Sepals 5, con- nate at very base, +/- unequal especially in width, quincuncial, persistent in fruit. Corolla of 5 unequally connate petals, zygo- morphic, curved in bud, 2-lipped at anthe- sis, +/- fleshy, white to pale green, the outer surface usually +/- pubescent (at least in bud or on lobes), the inner surface glabrous at base, woolly at throat and to a variable distance on base of lobes within, the lobes imbricate, +/- cucullate at apex, the innermost one connate to a lesser extent, often appar- ently trough-shaped, apparently in the up- per (abaxial) position, the others forming a 4-lobed, +/- recurved lip. Androecium of 2 fertile stamens and 3 staminodes; filaments of fertile stamens and staminodes flattened in cross-section for all of their length except for the free apical part, free from each other, the fertile filaments free from corolla at base and adherent at the throat and sometimes also for some distance above the throat by abaxial woolly tomentum, adaxially gla- brous at base and barbate at throat, with apex free from corolla, the staminodes usually free from corolla at base and adherent at the throat and sometimes also for some distance above the throat by abaxial tomentum and with apex free from corolla or adnate to corolla and arising at the throat; anthers oblong or narrow-ovate, basifixed, connate, glabrous or villous, with conspic- uous, asymmetric, usually unilaterally curved-attenuate, free, flap-like appendages at base, the connective gland-dotted, gla- brous or villous abaxially; pollen grains 5- 6-colporate, spherical or prolate-spheroidal, large (in the sense of Erdtman, 1971), the exine reticulate. Disc cupular, shorter to taller than ovary, glabrous. Ovary of 5, free carpels united only at the base and by the single style; stigma subcapitate. Fruit of 1- 5 mericarps, free or slightly connate at the base, each elliptic to obovate, rounded dorsally, beaked (hirsuta) or not beaked, ventrally dehiscent. Seeds 1 per carpel, oblong, smooth, glabrous, sometimes falling with membranous part of endocarp attached, the testa leathery. Embryo curved, the hypo- cotyl apical, the cotyledons bilobed, conduplicate, subequal, usually thick, stiff, gland-dotted.
bibliographicCitation: Kallunki, Jacquelyn A. 1994. Revision of Raputia Aubl. (Cuspariinae, Rutaceae). Brittonia. 46: 279-295.

description: Shrub or small tree without raphides, the hairs with incomplete septa. Stipules interpetiolar, entire, persistent. Leaves opposite or ternate, petiolate, the blade entire. Inflorescences terminal, pedunculate, paniculate-thyrsoid with cymose branches. Flowers homostylous or heterostylous, 5-merous, pedicellate; hypanthium turbinate, biloculate; placenta V-shaped to cordiform with indefinite ovules; calyx tubular with 4-5 (7) small lobes or rarely entire, the interior surface of the tube charged with 2-7 small glands opposite each sinus near the base, persistent on the fruit; corolla white, salverform, valvate and reduplicate, with the distal 2/3-3/4 of the lobes carinate and the proximal portion flat triangular, sloping from the keel to the base; stamens alternate with the corolla lobes, included, the filaments adnate to the inner face of the corolla tube and departing from it ca '/4 of the way up to slightly beyond the middle, the anthers free or coherent, 4-thecate, narrowly oblong to linear, obtuse or cordate at the base, with an extended connective narrowly acute to very narrowly acute at the apex, glabrous, opening by full-length lateral slits, dorsifixed well below the middle, the pollen weakly prolate spheroidal 18-21 jtm in equatorial and polar diam, 3- or 4-colporate; disc circular, entire, filling the space between the base of the corolla and the base of the style; style straight or straight with a swelling above the base, glabrous, the stigma bilobate, included, its lobes lanceolate, appressed, glabrous, in homostylous plants amid the anthers and in heterostylous plants either above (in pin flowers) or below (in thrum flowers). Fruit fleshy, indehiscent, green turning orange and then black as it matures, the seeds many, globular, the seed coat cells (fide M. C. G. Kirkbride, 1976) polygonal with small pits scattered in the internal cell walls, the lateral walls thick, the external wall smooth.
bibliographicCitation: Kirkbride, Joseph H., Jr. 1979. Rariteae, an overlooked genus of the Rubiaceae. Brittonia. 31: 299-312.

description: Trees, when pubescent the hairs incompletely septate; stipules divided, persistent. Inflorescences terminal, paniculate-thyrsoid with cymose branches. Corolla salverform, its lobes 5, valvate; stamens 5, inserted at the base of the corolla tube; stigma bilobate. Ovary bilocular, the ovules numerous on a cordiform or V-shaped placenta. Fruit globose; seeds (Fig. 10) 0.2-0.6 mm in diam; seed coat (Figs. 11, 12) with polygonal cells, 66-119 (89.9) x 39-77 (69.4) µm, with small pits scattered in the internal cell walls (Figs. 11, 12), more than 50 pits per cell, less than 1.3 µm in diam, the external cell wall smooth, the lateral walls thick, 15-18 µm thick.
bibliographicCitation: Kirkbride, M. C. G. 1979. Review of the neotropical Isertieae (Rubiaceae). Brittonia. 31: 313-332.

description: Raveniae affinis. Sepala 5 corollae tubam fere aequantia, 3 interiora linearia, 2 exteriora ovato-lanceolata. Corollae tubulosae lobi paulo inaequales. Filamenta connata in tubum ad basin corollae adnatum sursum liberum. Staminodia 3 subulata arete approximata, 2 lateralia creseentiformia, 1 medianum rectum. Stamina fertilia 2 brevissime stipitata, lateraliter conliata, basi intus saccato-producta, apice acuta. Discus infundibuliformis obscure 5-lobatus. Ovaria 5. Ovula in quoque loculo 2, unum tantum fertile. Capsula longitudinaliter dehiscens endocarpium exhibens. Stylus gracilis, apice radiatim 5-lobatus. Flores sessiles in spicam disticham arete confertam aggregati.
bibliographicCitation: Gleason, Henry A. & Killip, E. P. 1939. The flora of Mount Auyan-Tepui, Venezuela. Brittonia. 3: 141-204. f. 1-5.

description: Small trees with pinnately compound leaves, the leaflets alternate, the rachis narrowly winged; infloreseenee a complex mixed paniele, frequently with many of the buds not developing into flowers; flowers complete, slightly perigynous, and bearing a 10-lobed glandular ring or disk; sepals 5, petaloid, persistent through fruiting; petals 5, surpassing the sepals, soon deciduous; stamens 10; carpels 1-3, commonly 2, distinct, borne on a short gynophore; styles basal or nearly so; ovules 2 in each carpel, commonly only one maturing; fruit drupaceous.
bibliographicCitation: Cronquist, Arthur J. 1944. Studies in the Simaroubaceae--IV. Resumé of the American genera. Brittonia. 5: 128-147.

description: Perennis stolonifera, dioica; ligula membranacea, apice erosa; spiculae 2-3(-4), appressae, obovato-lanceolatae, 3-8-florae; glumae persistentes, obovato-lanceolatae, prima quam secunda 1/4 brevior, nerviis paucibus-pluribus indistinctis, marginibus seariosis; lodiculae 2, parvae, cuneatae. Spicutla masculina: glumae glabrae; lemmata glabra, arete imbricata, appressa, acuta, basin versus latiora, nerviis paucibus-pluribus indistinctis, marginibus scariosis; palea lemma aequans, glabra, a latere visa angusta et linearis; antherae 3, inaequales. Spicula feminea: glumae ad basin pilosae, supra basin glabrae; lemmnata ad basin pilosa, superne glabra arete imbricata, appressa, acuta, basin versus latiora, nerviis paucibus-pluribus indistinctis, marginibus scariosa; palea lemma aequans, a latere visa superne angusta, linearis, glabra, ad basin latiora, pilosa; caryopsis plus minusve recta angulata, in rostello terminans; embryo ca 2/5 partem fructus aequans.
bibliographicCitation: Soderstrom, Thomas R. & Decker, Henry F. 1964. Reederochloa, a new genus of dioecious grasses from Mexico. Brittonia. 16: 334-339.

description: Erect, herbaceous or suffrutescent perennials, with one to several simple or branched shoots arising annually from the bases of previous shoots, from a woody crown, from horizontal-spreading roots, or from tuberous roots. Stems becoming woody or spongy below; subterete about the middle with 4 well-defined faces (sides), their edges inconspicuously to prominently winged; the faces flat to convex and essentially equal, or one pair of opposing faces flat to concave and much narrower than the other pair of convex or rounded faces; sometimes conspicuously grooved near the summit; internodes glabrous or with few to many straight, scattered, horizontal-spreading, glandular hairs; the nodes with tufts of soft, glandular hairs, or with a ring of short, straight, non-glandular, ascending or appressed hairs (rarely glabrous or with divergent bristles). Leaves opposite, with (1-)3-5(-7) palmate veins, the lateral nerves, when present, arcuate; petio- late to sessile, and with serrulate to serrate (sometimes distantly so), frequently ciliate margins. Flowers perigynous, ca. 1.5 to 7 cm in diameter, solitary or more commonly borne in open (rarely condensed), few- to many-flowered cymes; the bracts similar to the leaves or conspicuously smaller, persistent (rarely decidu- ous). Petals 4, distinct, oblique, commonly rose to purple, occasionally white (rarely yellow), fugacious, variable in shape from rotund to oblong, obovate or cuneate, with obtuse to truncate, usually aristate apices, convolute in the bud, at right angles to the axis, reflexed or ascending at anthesis, alternating with the sepals, glabrous or with few scattered usually glandular hairs near the margins on the abaxial surfaces. Hypanthium more or less urceolate, composed of two apparent layers, a thin, inner layer which is slightly shorter and terminates abruptly as a torus bearing the petals and stamens, and an outer layer which bears the calyx-lobes at its summit; the body or lower globose portion of the hypanthium somewhat ventricose, enclosing all or the greater portion of the capsule, constricted above up to 1/2 (rarely to 1/4) the diameter of the body and ex- tended upward as a neck for a distance nearly equaling to exceeding the length of the body, sometimes abruptly expanded above. Calyx-lobes erect, spreading or strongly recurved, semicircular, deltoid to lanceolate, the tips obtuse, acute to acuminate (rarely aristate). Stamens 8, isomorphic, superficially appearing in one whorl but actually composed of an outer antesepalous whorl and an inner ante- petalous whorl. Anthers i-celled at anthesis, basifixed, introrse, fused to the connective their entire length or free from it basally, yellow (occasionally turn- ing orange upon drying), smooth, or papillose to various degrees (rarely entirely so); short (1-3 mm long) or long [(4-)5-11 mm in length]; ascending, or declinate and more or less symmetrically oriented in such a way that they tend to be paral- lel and declined toward one side of the flower, straight or slightly curved to sigmoid, frequently inflated at the base, gradually tapering toward the apex, dehiscing by a large pore nearly equaling the diameter of the tip of the anther or by a small pore ca. 1/3 the diameter of the anther tip, the pore located on the adaxial surface of the anther near the apex; filaments straight, erect, glabrous, ca. as long as the anther, flattened dorsiventrally, frequently geniculate near the point of insertion with the anther, the connective extending nearly to the apex of the anther, usually appendaged anteriorly to the insertion of the anther with a short spur or thread-like filament up to ca. 2 mm long; stamens inflexed in the hypanthium before anthesis, the apices of the anthers (when long) extending into interstices between the hypanthium and the free apical portion of the ovary, the adaxial surface of the anthers facing the hypanthial wall, and the abaxial surface adjacent to the ovary wall. Stigma subcapitate, the style exserted to or beyond the anthers, straight, curved to sigmoid, usually strongly declined to one side of the flower with the stigma below the anthers. Ovary quadricarpellate, quadri- locular, partially adnate to the hypanthium, sessile, glabrous or occasionally with a few glandular hairs at the apex; maturing into a globose, subglobose, pyriform or flask-shaped capsule with loculicidal dehiscence; septations semicircular to lunate; placenta axillary, pedicellate, projecting well into the locules; ovules numerous. Seeds strongly curved to cochleate, less than 1 mm long (rarely oblong and exceeding 1 mm in length); seed coat white, brown to dark gray, nearly smooth, muriculate, papillose, verrucose, ridged, or with low dome-shaped processes. Flowering from mid-spring into mid-fall.
bibliographicCitation: James, Charles W. 1956. A Revision of Rhexia (Melastomataceae). Brittonia. 8 (3): 201-230.

description: Arbores; pili dibrachiati, rarius simplices. Phyllotaxis ramorum fertilium regulatim spiralis. Foliorum lamina integra, subtus nec papillosa nec farinosa, glandulis praesertim secus nervum medianum, nonquam ad marginem dispersis. Thyrsi terminales, pro parte maxima rubri, identidem ramosi monoici. Cymularum mascularum 1- vel 3-florarum bracteae glandulosae vel eglandulosae; bracteolae aliquantum reductae; flores pedicellati articulati, ante anthesin axi appressi per anthesin effusi; sepala connata; stamina 2-6, filamentis brevibus basi connatis. Pollinis grana apud R. macrophyllum tricolporata semitectata reticulata. Flores foeminei breviter pedicellati tricarpellati, calyce tripartito saepe glanduloso, sepalis basi connatis; stylorum columna distincta. Fructus septiatque loculicidaliter dehiscentes, columella centrali conspicue trialata; mericarpiorum septa filum vasculare singulum furcatum praebentia; semina anatropa ecarunculata, testa pro parte reticulato-foveolata vel colliculata nec omnino laevia.
bibliographicCitation: Esser, Hans-Joachim. 1999. Rhodothyrsus, a new genus of Euphorbiaceae from tropical South America. Brittonia. 51: 170-180.

description: Trees. Latex white. Hairs brownish-yellowish, unicellular dibrachiate, rarely simple. Twigs smooth, not hollow; terminal ones alternate, not in whorls. Leaves alternate and in regular spirals, not congested. Stipules longer than wide, undivided, basally often glandular, caducous. Leaves with 3-22 cm long, eglandular, apically pulvinate petioles; blades narrowly ovate to elliptic, often conspicuously variable in size even on one twig, entire, adaxially eglandular, abaxially shiny, without papillae or cuticular folds, with laminar glands mostly close to or touching the primary vein; secondary veins eucamptodromous, at least when dry often conspicuously reddish, tertiary veins indistinctly percurrent to reticulate, smaller veins reticulate. Thyrses terminal, purplish or orange, 2-5-times branched, monoecious; lateral branches subtended by broadly triangular scaly bracts, these usually glandular or with separate glandular stipules; axes of branches hirsute-sericeous to glabrous. Bracts of staminate cymules membranaceous, eglandular or with minute cylindrical glands, sericeous. Staminate cymules 1- or 3-flowered; bracteoles of central flower usually present but small and inconspicuous; flowers always pedicellate, articulate, abaxially inclinate and appressed to the axis, spreading only at anthesis; sepals nearly completely united, without distinct lobes and therefore of uncertain number, open in bud; stamens 2-6, anthers free, filaments short and only basally connate. Pollen (only known in R. macrophyllus) semi-tectate reticulate. Pis- tillate cymules 1-flowered, on base of thyrse, sometimes absent; flowers with ped- icels 1-4 mm long; sepals 3, broadly tri- angular, basally fused for up to half of their length, usually with disciform glands ca. 1 mm long; ovary glabrous or hirsute, smooth, with 3 locules, often distinctly trigonal in section, stylar column present, stigmas very short, undivided, smooth. Fruits with short but distinct and hardly elongating pedicel; schizocarp circular to slightly transversely elliptic in outline, sulcate, 7-18 mm long, glabrous or hirsute, dry, smooth, dehiscing septicidally and loculicidally; persistent central columella with conspicuous wide wings, not splitting; pericarp thickness ca. 1:10 of mericarp length, septa with one often bifurcate vascular strand in upper half, basally with distinct triangular split. Seeds globose to slightly transversely elliptic, anatropous, ecarunculate; surface dry, brownish, heterogeneous and consisting of longitudinal stripes and patches of smooth cells and others of larger, distinctly sculptured cells of different color.
bibliographicCitation: Esser, Hans-Joachim. 1999. Rhodothyrsus, a new genus of Euphorbiaceae from tropical South America. Brittonia. 51: 170-180.

description: Hypanthium tubular or campanulate, pubescent to villous or hirsute; sepals triangular-subulate or linear-subulate, spreading or recurved, equaling or longer than the hypanthium; petals obovate, purple or white, conspicuous; sterile stamens 5, reduced to hairlike anthers and a minute connective; fertile stamens 5, the anthers nar- rowly ovoid, terminating in a long, slender, obliquely 1-pored beak, the connective conspicuously prolonged at base and terminating in a simple, 2-saccate, or 2-lobed small appendage below the filament; ovary 3-5-celled, usually smooth; style elongate; stigma punctiform. Flowers short-peduncled, closely invested by the upper leaves, few or numerous, in the latter case forming a large leafy panicle; leaves and stems usually pubescent, villous, or hirsute, and often glandular.  About 40 species, most numerous in Brazil, and ranging north to Mexico.
bibliographicCitation: Gleason, Henry A. 1932. A Synopsis of the Melastomataceae of British Guiana. Brittonia. 1 (3): 127-184.

description: Two species. Perennial herbs or shrubs, procumbent, ascending, or erect. Leaves petiolate, the blades orbicular, ovate, or lanceolate, obtuse to acute, crenate or serrate; stipules linear. Flowers solitary in the leaf axils; pedicels slender; involucel absent; calyx deeply 5-lobed, accrescent and inflated in fruit, the lobes cordate-ovate, overlapping, apiculate; petals yellowish, with or without a purple spot at the base, slightly exceeding to twice as long as the calyx; androecium included, filamentiferous at apex; styles 8-14, the stigmas capitate. Fruits schizocarpic; mericarps 8-14, blackish, indurate, indehiscent, with a long obtuse rostrum, and with lateral walls notably reticulate fenestrate, the dorsal wall grooved; seeds solitary, minutely pubescent. 2n = 16 (one species).
bibliographicCitation: Fryxell, Paul A. 1997. The American genera of Malvaceae --- II. Brittonia. 49: 204-269.

description: Plantae procumbentes, ascendentes, vel erectae; calycibus fructificantibus accrescentibus vesicari- isque, in statu maturo herbaceis non brunneo-reticulatis; mericarpiis 8-14, denigratis, induratis, cum rostro elongato et obtuso et cum parietibus lateralibus insigniter reticulato-fenestratis.

description: Plants annual, herbaceous, erect, openly branched, slender-stemmed; principal leaves largely opposite, petioled, nmembraneous, subglabrous, oblong-ovate, serrate, obtuse to acute at base, subaculmiinate at apex; uppermost leaves reduced to pubeseent alternate lanceolate leafy bracts. Flowers small, in terminal racemes. Floral tube tubular-funnelform, deciduous, pubescent, especially the lower hairs gland-tipped. Sepals 4, linear-lanceolate, acute, divergent, rather bristly-pubeseent, more or less separate in anthesis, shorter than the floral tube, subequal. Petals 4, unguiculate, unequal, the blades strongly crinkled on the margins, the 2 posterior subequal, asymmetrically oblong-oblanceolate, 1 mm wide, subobtuse, with arcuate "gland" or tubercle at base of blade, the 2 anterior larger, but slightly unequal, suborbicular, 2.5 mm wide, obtuse. Stamens 2, apparently located on either side of the largest petal, one fertile, equaling the petals; filament stout, subfusiform; anther large, almost equaling the filament, dorsifixed, ovoid; second stamen a sterile staminode, expanded above into a suborbicular petaloid structure with terminal recurved subulate tip. Style stout, almost equaling the petals; stigma depressed-capitate; ovary glandular- puberulent and with some stiff non-glandular hairs, pedicelled, elongate, 4-loculed, axillary-placentate, with many ovules. Capsules oblong-fusiform, about as long as the subfiliform pedicels, rather thin-walled, 4-valved from apex. Seeds dark, narrow-obovoid, with few longitudinal ridges and also strongly transversely rugose.
bibliographicCitation: Munz, Philip A. 1961. The Lopezieae (Onagraceae). Brittonia. 13 (1): 73-90.

description: Dioecious trees; bark exfoliating in small, papery, longitudinal strips. Stipules interpetiolar, large, foliose, membranous, long-pubescent, persistent. Leaf blades obovate to broadly obovate; domatia absent. Inflorescences terminal. Pistillate flowers short-pedicellate, solitary. Staminate flowers long-pedicellate, in terminal, cymose, 5-9-flowered inflorescences. Calyx 6-8-lobed; tube short-campanulate; lobes contorted, large, foliose, membranous, persistent. Corolla campanulate, 12-15-lobed, greenish yellow; the tube pubescent inside and outside; the lobes contorted, ovate, pointed at apex. Stamens alternate to the petals, included, subsessile; anthers narrowly oblong, dorsifixed near the base, dehiscing by longitudinal slits; filaments attachec near mouth of corolla, extremely short, glabrous throughout. Style included, minutely ribbed; style branches 2, thick-clavate; stylk of staminate flowers pushing through the anthers functioning as a means of secondary pollen presentation (pollen is presented on the outer surface of style branches). Ovary 2-celled, with many seeds per locule inserted on the central placenta. Fruit terminal, solitary, oblong-ovoid, bilocular. with many seeds per locule, crowned by the persistent membranous calyx, exocarp thick coriaceous-woody, endocarp hard-fleshy. Seeds horizontally inserted, in one rank pei locule, dorsiventrally flattened.
bibliographicCitation: Delprete, Piero G. 1999. Riodocea (Rubiaceae, Gardenieae), a new genus from the Brazilian Atlantic forest. Brittonia. 51: 15-23.

description: Shrubs or small trees 1-7 m tall, unarmed. Branches bearing ±decussate brachyblasts with crowded leaves; long-shoots sericeous or glabrescent. Stipules fused at base, with interpetiolar lobes, persistent, lobes broadly triangular, rigid with two ridges converging into a subulate apex, membranaceous in between and at margins, abaxial surface slightly sericeous or glabrous, adaxial surface with colleters and hairs toward base; colleters many, conical, ? stalked, diameter of central axis exceeding palisade cells, 0.5-1 mm long. Leaves decussate, subsessile to petiolate, leaves on long-shoots often with longer petioles than those of short-shoots; petioles sericeous; leaf blades with ±reticulate venation, secondary veins ascendent, mostly not anastomosing; margin entire, crystal sand abundant in both palisade and parenchyma tissues. Flowers terminal on brachyblasts, sessile, solitary, hermaphroditic, 5(-6)-merous, fragrant. Calyx tube sericeous outside, with scattered hairs and colleters or almost glabrous on inside upper parts, glabrous or subglabrous to sericeous from a ±dense ring of hairs and colleters at base; colleters many, of the same appearance as those on the stipules; calyx lobes subulate, narrowly triangular, adaxially sericeous, sericeous abaxially, with a few hairs or glabrous toward base. Corolla white, salverform; tube narrowly cylindrical, almost glabrous to densely antrorsely sericeous externally, antrorsely sericeous internally in upper part, glabrous or subglabrous below, tube widened distally; lobes ovate to narrowly triangular, apex acuminate, base obtuse to truncate, contorted to the left in bud. Anthers free, attached sessilely to subsessilely in the distal part of the tube, semi-exserted, dorsi-fixed just below the middle; linear-oblong, darkened connective tissue covering abaxial surface, apical appendage absent or minute; thecae not partitioned, dehiscent by longitudinal slits; pollen in monads, 4- 7-zonoporate or 5-13-pantoporate; style hairy on upper 1/2 to 1/3, glabrous below, hairs unicellular, thin walled, stigma ±semi-exserted, 2-lobed, free and clearly separate, ovate to oblong, furrowed adaxially; disk annular, glabrous; ovary 1-locular with 2 placentas fused toward base, or 2-locular; ovules numerous in four rows on the two parietal placentas. Fruits indehiscent, spherical to cylindrical, crowned by the persistent calyx, sericeous when young, later sparsely sericeous; immature fruits green with pale green to white longitudinal stripes, mature fruits yellowish to orange, exocarp thin; mesocarp to 1 mm thick, with brown idioblasts and crystal sand; endocarp thin, cells sclerified, transversely elongated; seeds flattened, ±lenticular, irregularly elliptic in outline, imbedded in placental pulp.
bibliographicCitation: Gustafsson, C. G. R. 1998. The neotropical Rosenbergiodendron (Rubiaceae, Gardenieae). Brittonia. 50: 452-466.

description: Scandent shrubs, when pubescent the hairs incompletely septate; stipules entire. Inflorescences axillary, capitulate or corymbiform. Corolla hypocrateriform, its lobes 4 or 5, valvate; stamens 4 or 5, inserted in the upper half of the corolla tube; stigma 4- or 5-lobed. Ovary 4 or 5 locular, the ovules numerous on a cordiform placenta. Fruit ovoid; seeds (Fig. 15) 0.4-0.6 mm long, 0.4-0.5 mm in diam, foveolate; seed coat (Fig. 16) with iregularly rectangular cells, 69-111 (87.6) x 15-24 (20.1) ,um, moderate size pits in both lateral and internal walls (Fig. 16), 28-50 pits per cell, 2-3 µm in diam, the lateral walls moderately thick, 1.5-2.5 µm thick.

description: As Alsine Gaertn. was antedated by Alsine L., Doctor Small changed the name to Alsinopsis. He overlooked the fact that there were several published generic names available for the genus. Fernald and others have accepted Minuartia L. as the oldest, but neither the type of that genus, nor the two species added later by Loeffling, be- long to it according to the generic concepts of Small, myself, and per- haps others. The oldest valid name is evidently Sabtlina Reich.
bibliographicCitation: Rydberg, Per A. 1934. Taxonomic notes on the flora of the prairies and plains of central North America. Brittonia. 1: 79-104.

description: Lianas or shrubs or slender trees, usually with the upper branches scandent, glabrous throughout or essentially so, the branchlets subterete, often swollen or somewhat flattened at nodes; leaves opposite or alternate, the petioles rugose, canaliculate; infloreseence axillary or arising from defoliate branehlets, often replete with mucilaginous fibers, thyrsoid-paniculate or eymose or crowded-racemose or fasciculate, the branchlets subtended by small bracts; flowers congested or loosely arranged, often large for the family; sepals 5, usually broadly imbricate, often unequal (inner ones largest), broadly ovate to deltoid, often seariose and erosulous at margins; petals 5 (rarely 6), narrowly imbricate, usually rotate at anthesis, rounded at apex, entire or erosulous at margins; disk carnose (rarely thin-carnose), annular-pulvinate (rarely cupuliform), truncate-conical or flattened; stamens 3 (rarely 4), suberect to sharply reflexed, the filaments ligulate, usually thin- carnose and slightly broadened toward base, the anthers basifixed, 2-celled, snmall, trainsversely ellipsoid or reniform or obrhomboid or ovate-deltoid, the clefts extrorse or apical, horizontal or oblique, con- flueht or apically confluent (rarely merely continguous); ovary depressed-conical, often subtrigonous, usually deeply immersed in disk and connate to it, taperinig to a short carnose subulate truncate style, the stigmas obscure; locules 3, the ovules 2-8 per locule, collateral or superposed or in superposed pairs; fruits subglobose or ellipsoid, the pericarp coriaceous, the dissepiments soon evanescent, the seeds several to many, imbedded in mucilaginous pulp, oblong, angled.
bibliographicCitation: Smith, Albert C. 1940. The American species of Hippocrateaceae. Brittonia. 3: 341-555. f. 1-12.

description: Shrubs, rarely tree-like, to 10 m high. Leaf blades entire or toothed, glabrous or pu- bescent, glaucous or not beneath. Staminate aments precocious to coetaneous, sessile or with floriferous branchlets to 2 cm long, stamens 2. Pistillate aments precocious to coetaneous, sessile or with floriferous branch- lets to 3 cm long. Capsule glabrous (occasionally pubescent in S. myricoides), style 0.1-2(2.5) mm long, stipe 0.3-5 mm long. Floral bract tawny, light brown, dark brown, or rarely black, persistent in fruit.
bibliographicCitation: Dorn, Robert D. 1995. A taxonomic study of Salix section Cordatae subsection Luteae (Salicaceae). Brittonia. 47: 160-174.

description: Hypanthium tubular, much elongate in fruit, 10-ribbed, with ob- scure sepals; petals small, acute; stamens 10, essentially isomorphic, the anthers subulate; ovary free, 3-celled, 3-lobed and depressed at the summit; style elongate, with punctiform stigma. Smooth herbs with thin leaves, bearing one to a few terminal or subterminal race- miform secund eymes of sessile or short-pedicelled flowers, the axis elonigating and straightening in fruit. Four species in tropical South America.
bibliographicCitation: Gleason, Henry A. 1932. A Synopsis of the Melastomataceae of British Guiana. Brittonia. 1 (3): 127-184.

description: Shrubs or perennial (rarely biennial or annual) herbs, usually with aromatic foliage. Leaves opposite, decussate, petiolate to subsessile; margin crenate to serrate, sometimes deeply lobed or divided. Inflorescence of 1- to many-flowered verticillas- trate cymes positioned along branched or unbranched indeterminate axes. Calyx campanulate to tubular, bilabiate, unmodified to slightly accrescent in fruit (rarely strongly accrescent); upper lip entire, or 2-3-lobed, lower lip 2-lobed. Corolla tubular, bilabiate; tube straight or curved; upper lip entire or bifid, straight or curved, usually concave; lower lip 3-lobed, central lobe usually larger than the lateral lobes. Fertile stamens 2, epipetalous; anterior theca large and fertile, posterior theca much smaller and fertile or sterile; connective often greatly elongated; staminodes usually present. Style gynobasic, filiform, apically 2-lobed. Nutlets 4, spherical to ellipsoidal, smooth.
bibliographicCitation: Torke, Benjamin M. 2000. A revision of Salvia sect. Ekmania (Lamiaceae). Brittonia. 52: 265-302.

description: Dioecious pandanoid trees to 20 m tall or more, branching at last; leaves set in four spiral rows, elonigate, coriaceous, anid stoutly armed; proproots none; aerial roots forming a fille mesh or network at the base of the trunk; inflorescence paniculate, terminal, bracteate; male flowers pedicellate, the perianth a short entire undulate-margined cupule; stamens numerous, the filaments nar- rowing at the tip, anthers oblong, dorsally affixed; pollen ellipsoid, minutely papillate; female flowers shortly pedicellate, the perianth free, somewhat fleshy, entire and truncate or irregularly 3- to 4-lobed; staminodia none; ovary fleshy, of many (10-80) carpels, these one-seeded, arranged in a biseriate sinuous row; stigmas sessile, subopposite in pairs, with a ventral sutural pore, discoid to somewhat horseshoe-shaped; ovules anatropous; fruit a succulent polypyrenoid drupe, the pyrenes flat, osseous; endosperm copious and oily; embryo conic, basal.
bibliographicCitation: Stone, Benjamin C. M. 1961. The genus Sararanga (Pandanaceae). Brittonia. 13: 212-224.

description: Undershrubs or perennial herbs, with opposite, entire, estipulate, sessile or petioled leaves. Flowers small, in loose eymules, these disposed in a thyrse or a more or less effuse panicle. Sepals normally 5 (rarely 6), imbricated, per- sistent. True petals absent. Staminodia opposite the sepals and just as many, hyaline, more or less petaloid at least below, at apex entire or bifid. True stamens normally 10, the five opposite the sepals each adnate to the base of a staminodiuml; anthers short, oblong, versatile; filaments capillary. Ovary 1-celled, the numer- ous ovules affixed to a short, central placenta. Styles 3 or often 4 or 5, filiformn, their clavate apex stigmatose all around. Capsule splitting into as many entire valves as there are styles. Seeds reniform to orbicular, subglobose or compressed, with a coriaceous, now rugose or muricate now almost smooth testa, estrophiolate. Embryo anniular, surrounding a mealy albumen.
bibliographicCitation: Sherff, Earl E. 1945. Revision of the genus Schiedea Cham. & Schlecht. Brittonia. 5: 308-336.

description: Plants medium-sized in golden-green mats. Stems creeping, not complanate-foliate; in cross-section with 2-4 rows of small thick-walled cells surrounding larger, thinner-walled cells, central strand present, of small, thin-walled cells; pseudoparaphyllia foliose; rhizoids stem-borne, finely roughened. Branch and stem leaves similar, erect-spreading, those of the stem slightly larger and broader, ovate, acuminate, the apex mostly twisted, once or twice; margins plane above, recurved or plane below, serrate to serrulate almost to base; costa single, extending to about 3/4 the leaf length, projecting as a small spine at the end; upper cells linear to long-hexagonal, smooth, thin-walled; alar cells irregularly short-rectangular, extending somewhat up the margins, sometimes reaching the costa, if not then the juxtacostal cells at insertion ± porose. Autoicous. Perichaetial leaves erect with recurved apices, oblong-lanceolate, long-acuminate; margins plane, serrulate; ecostate; upper cells linear, becoming short-rectangular toward the insertion. Setae elongate, erect, smooth, reddish, often darkening with age; capsules erect to sub-erect, yellowish-red, often darkening with age, cylindric, gradually tapering to seta; exothecial cells rectangular, firm-walled, becoming gradually shorter in 1-3 rows toward the mouth; annulus of 1-2 rows of rectangular, firm-walled cells, readily deciduous; operculum obliquely rostrate; peristome double, exostome teeth lanceolate, shouldered, bordered, on front surface cross-striolate below, papillose above, with projecting trabeculae at back; endostome with a medium-height basal membrane, segments narrow, keeled, perforate, finely papillose, cilia none or sometimes rudimentary. Calyptrae cucullate, smooth, naked. Spores spherical, finely papillose.
bibliographicCitation: Buck, William R. 1985. A revision of Schimperella (Brachytheciaceae). Brittonia. 37: 36-40.

description: Undershrubs to tall trees. Branches with resin-ducts in the cortex, numerous, very slender to thick but never staghorn-like, pungent or not, glabrous to densely pilose, the pith small. Leaves simple or compound, small to large, membranaceous to thick-coriaceous, glabrous to densely pilose, the margins entire, subentire, crenulate, dentate, or serrate, flat to strongly revolute; rachis (when present) alate; leaflets sessile or subsessile. Infloreseence a spike-like pseudoraceme, a slightly branched panicle, or a much branched large panicle, glabrous to densely short-pilose. Flowers many, small. Bracts usually deltoid or deltoid-ovate, rarely deltoid-lanceolate, glabrous to densely pilose on the dorsal surface, usually more or less densely ciliate on the margin with simple trichomes, sometimes with clavate glandular hairs intermixed. Pedicels usually slender, 1-4 times as long as the flowers, with a prominent abscission ring one-third to one-half of the length from the base, usually more densely pubescent below the abscission disk, the pedicel gradually or abruptly enlarging at the apex. Sepals 4-5, deltoid, ovate, or rotund, glabrous to densely pilose on the dorsal surface, usually more or less densely ciliate on the margin with simple trichomes, sometimes with clavate glandular hairs intermixed. Petals 4-5, lanceolate to broadly ovate, truncate, 2-4 times as long as the sepals, glabrous or rarely with a few simple trichomes near the base or rarely ciliate with simple hairs. Stamens 8-10, those alternating with the petals almost as long as the petals or sometimes longer, those opposite the petals one-half to two-thirds as long as the petals, filaments somewhat enlarged toward the base, the anthers ovate to oblong; stamens in the pistillate flowers somewhat smaller than in the staminate. Disk thick, saucer-shaped, with lobes as many as the stamens and alternating with themii. Pistil tricarpellary, the stigmas three, inverted V-shaped to subglobose, the styles three, free above, united the lower half of their length, the ovary one-celled, with a single suspended ovule. Fruit a small drupe, the exocarp thin, chartaceous, shining (but often with a few simple trichomes), lavender to deep red, separating from the mesocarp at maturity, the mesocarp thin, resinous, adhering to the bony endocarp.
bibliographicCitation: Barkley, F. A. 1944. Schinus L. Brittonia. 5: 160-198. f. 1-22.

description: Caespitose or rhizomatous perennials, with rounded or compressed and keeled sheaths and flat or folded, infrequently terete, blades. Flowering culms usually much-branched, each branch or branchlet terminating in a single pedunculate raceme. Spikelets appressed to the rachis or somewhat divergent at maturity. Sessile spikelet fertile, awned. Pedicelled spikelet narrow, neuter, reduced but usually present. Chromosome numbers mostly 2n = 20 and 40.
bibliographicCitation: Gould, Frank W. 1967. The Grass Genus Andropogon in the United States. Brittonia. 19: 70-76.

description: Openly branched pubescent shrub. Leaves opposite or alternate, ovate to lance-ovate, rather coarsely pubescent on both sides, the principal ones short- petioled, shallowly sinuate-serrulate, with about 15-20 principal veins on each side of the midrib, more or less cuneate at base, subacuminate at apex, those of the infloreseence reduced to foliose bracts, oblong-ovate to ovate, entire, acute, 6-10-veined oil each side of the midrib, more finely and densely viscid-pubescent. Branchlets slender, terete, ending in foliose several-flowered racemes grouped in large drooping panicles. Pedicels slender, spreading, coarsely and finely pubescent, mostly longer thaii the subtending bracts. Floral tube crimson, tubular- funnelform, coarsely and finely pubeseelnt. Sepals lance-linear, crimson, sub-equal, aeuliminate, pubescent without, the 3 upper reflexed, the fourth projectingl forward. Petals nlarrowly linear, much shorter than the sepals, subequal. Stamens 2, united in the lower half to the style to form a long-exserted red column. Posterior stamen red, sterile, expanded at the free apex into a petaloid apiculate longitudinally folded portion. Anterior stamen fertile, red, glabrous, with a bilocular elongate anther. Style retrorsely pubescent; stigma subcapitate and umbilicate. Capsule globose to ellipsoid, 4-loculed, loculicidal by 4 valves, many-seeded. Seeds incurved-ovoid, minute, dark, irregularly muriculate.

description: About 100 species. Perennial herbs or subshrubs, erect or prostrate, glabrous or pubescent, sometimes viscid. Leaves petiolate to subsessile, the blades ovate (sometimes lobed), elliptic, rhombic, or linear, usually dentate. Flowers solitary in the leaf axils, in axillary glomnerules, or in dense or open terminal inflorescences; pedicels shorter than to much longer than the caly- ces; involucel absent; calyx 5-lobed, often 10-ribbed at the base and plicate in bud; corolla white, yellow, orangeish, rose, or purplish, sometimes with a dark red center; androecium included, usually pallid, filamentiferous at apex; styles 5-14, the stig mas capitate. Fruits schizocarpic, glabrous or pubescent; mericarps 5-14, usually indurate, usually laterally reticulate, indehis- cent below with well-differentiated dorsal wall, indehiscent or dehiscent apically, usually with 2 apical spines more or less well developed or muticous; seeds solitary, glabrous. Two series: 2n = 14, 28; 2n = 16, 32 (see commentary in the Introduction).
bibliographicCitation: Fryxell, Paul A. 1997. The American genera of Malvaceae --- II. Brittonia. 49: 204-269.

description: Two species. Shrubs ca. 3 m tall, densely pubescent with yellowish stellate (often stipitate) hairs. Leaves petiolate, the blades ovate or slightly 3-lobed, cordate, irregularly crenate-serrate, acute or acuminate, densely pubescent. Inflorescences axillary or terminal with subcorymbose branching, the flowers subsessile and congested at the ends of the branches; involucel absent; calyx deeply divided, densely pubescent externally, glabrous internally; petals ca. 1 cm long, white or lavender, bearded on claw; staminal column glabrous. Fruits oblate, glabrous, enclosed in calyx; mericarps 10- 12, 3-4 mm long, short-apiculate, trigonal in cross section; seeds solitary, glabrous. 2n = 10.
bibliographicCitation: Fryxell, Paul A. 1997. The American genera of Malvaceae --- II. Brittonia. 49: 204-269.

description: Frutices pilis stellatis luteolis dense obtectis; laminis foliorum ovatis vel leniter 3-lobulatis; inflorescentiis axillaribus vel terminalibus ramificantibus subcorym bosae; calycibus profunde partitis; petalis violaceis vel albidis; fructibus glabris, mericarpiis 10-12 in sectione transversali trigonis, pariete dorsali a parietibus lateralis differentibus; seminibus solitariis.

description: Trees, shrubs, or suffrutescent plants with the leaves all basal; leaves pinnately compound, with usually opposite leaflets, in one species only the terminal leaflet present; inflorescence a simple or mixed panicle; pedicels not jointed, or sometimes jointed at the base; flowers perfect; sepals 4-5, united at the base or to above the middle; petals 4-5, distinct, pubescent, more or less spreading at anthesis; stamens twice as many as the petals, each bearing a narrow more or less hairy appendage which may be attached throughout its length or merely joined at the base; gynoecium borne on an evident disk or gynophore; carpels 4-5, weakly united, each bearing a solitary ovule; style 1, but the part from each carpel discernible; stigma capitate or slightly lobed; fruit of several distinct drupes, sometimes only one maturing.
bibliographicCitation: Cronquist, Arthur J. 1944. Studies in the Simaroubaceae--IV. Resumé of the American genera. Brittonia. 5: 128-147.

description: Trees or shrubs with alternate pinnately compound leaflets; dioecious; inflorescence a complex mixed panicle, the staminate larger and with more numerous flowers than the pistillate; sepals 5, occasionally 4 or 6, united at the base; petals 5, occasionally 4 or 6, distinct; stamens appendaged at the base, 10, occasionally 8 or 12, in the pistillate flowers much reduced or absent; carpels 5, occasionally 4 or 6, weakly united, with a short common style and divergent stigmas; the staminate flowers with the gynophore present but the carpels absent; ovules I in each carpel; fruit of several distinct drupes.

description:
Hypanthium campanulate or tubular; sepals triangular, erect, persistent; petals pink or purple; perfect stamens 4; imperfect stamens 4 or 0; anthers broadly oblong, ovate, or subrotund, termi- niating in a wide 1-pored beak which equals the anther or is partially or almost wholly reduced; connective prolonged, nearly equaling the anther, and bituberculate at base, or not prolonged; ovary wholly superior, 2-celled, smooth; style filiform, the stigma not expanded; capsule subglobose to obovoid or short-cylindric, 2-4-valved. Slen- der, low, simple or sparingly branched herbs or half-shrubs, with minute flowers and small leaves, mostly of moist or sandy, sunny situations.

Of the 18 known species, 13 occur in Brazil, chiefly in the southern part, 1 in Colombia, and 4 in the Guianas. The genus is similar and closely related to Poteranthera.

description: The genus Solenidiopsis was established by Senghas (1986) to contain S. tigroides (C. Schweinf.) Senghas, a species previously placed in an overly broadly defined Odontoglossum Kunth. Solenidiopsis is characterized by a bilobed stigma and prominent column wings. Subsequently, a second species was added to the genus (Senghas, 1989; Bennett & Christenson, 1993). In addition to the two species proposed here, we are aware of at least one additional, undescribed Peruvian species. To date, the genus remains endemic to Peru.

description: Sophia was a pre-Linnean genus used by Linnaeus in 1735 but abandoned in 1753, later reinstated by Adanson and by Gilibert, and used in association with specific names by the latter and by numerous other authors.In the publication of Descrtrainit, Webb & Berthelot constituted it with two sections, each containing a single species, Sisymbrium Irio L. and S. millefolia. There is nothing to indicate in what respect the genus differs from Sisymbrium. In fact, S. Irio L. is, in my opinion, a good species of Sisymnbriurn. In the introduction Webb and Berthelot made a remark which might suggest that S. Sophia was re- garded as the type of Descurainia, but the section containing Irio is placed first, and S. Sophia L. was not even transferred to Descurainia. Descuraina. was used only by Des Moulins, before it was adopted by Prantl, in Engler & Prantl 's Pflanzenfamilien in the sense of S. Sophia L. and its relatives. Under the circumstances there is no reason why Descurainia should be conserved for Sisymbrittm Sophia and its allies, being a composite genus made by merging the two genera, Sophia andl Irio.
